phrases.text: At four in the afternoon on 16 October 1906,
the town of Köpenick was already in an uproar.
An extra sheet, the Cöpenicker Dampfboot Extrablatt,
put it in one line: since four o'clock,
the town had been in the greatest agitation.
The Berliner Zeitung quoted that line in September 2026,
and it reported that hundreds of people had
gathered in front of the town hall.
Inside, the mayor was under arrest.
The man giving the orders was a shoemaker with
no right to give any orders at all,
and he was wearing a captain's uniform.
Picture the crowd outside the building.
To understand how a shoemaker came to command a town hall,
you have to go back to a prison cell,
long before that afternoon.
The man was Wilhelm Voigt.
He was born on 13 February 1849 in Tilsit,
in East Prussia, the son of a shoemaker,
and he learned the trade young. He also learned prison young.
At fourteen he got his first short jail term,
and the decades that followed brought more convictions,
for theft and for forgery.
The heaviest sentence followed an attempt in 1890,
when he and a former cellmate tried to
break into the court cash office at Wongrowitz,
a town in what is now Poland.
The court in Gnesen handed him fifteen more years in a penitentiary,
a Zuchthaus, and the Deutsche Biographie dates that sentence to 1891.
He was in his early forties when it began.
He would not walk free again until early 1906,
and when he did, he had a long record,
a trade, and almost nothing else.
Early in 1906 he walked out of the
penitentiary and tried to start again.
He found work as a shoemaker in Wismar,
a Baltic port in Mecklenburg.
Within a few weeks, the Deutsche Biographie says,
the police expelled him from Mecklenburg. He went on to Berlin,
where the authorities were not going to make it easy.
A legal history article on the case cites a
freedom-of-movement law of 1867 as the relevant law.
It says he was repeatedly refused the
right to settle and take regular work,
and that he was finally expelled from Berlin and the surrounding towns.
German Wikipedia places him in Rixdorf and later in Friedrichshain,
living there without registering, which made every day he stayed unlawful.
Here is the trap, in plain terms.
Without a residence permit he could not take a regular job.
Without papers he could not get the one document
that would let him start again, a passport.
German Wikipedia notes that passports were issued by a district office in
Berlin, not by the town hall in Köpenick.
It also reports that Voigt claimed he had meant only to keep
the money and had really wanted a foreign passport,
and that the court called that claim entirely implausible.
Historians have argued about what drove him ever since.
A legal history article doubted that hardship was the whole motive,
and pointed to the town's cash and municipal bonds. Either way,
the man who walked into Köpenick that October had no papers,
no work and no legal address. He was free,
but only in the narrow sense that no cell was holding him.
On 8 October 1906 he began to build the disguise.
The Deutsche Biographie dates his first purchases to that day:
pieces of a captain's uniform, bought from dealers.
The Berlin museum exhibition says one of the
dealers sold secondhand military clothing.
The coat that came together was pieced together from parts, not tailored.
He also changed his face. The beard went,
and a white moustache took its place, according to the Deutsche Biographie.
A coat and a moustache do not make a captain on
their own, but they are enough to earn a second look.
What he still lacked was men.
A captain without soldiers is only a man in a costume,
so he set about finding some.
On 16 October, at midday,
he was near the military bath at Plötzensee,
where a squad of guard fusiliers was changing its guard.
German Wikipedia says he stopped the patrol,
placed ten or eleven men under his command,
and had a second group called in from a shooting range.
He told the men he was acting on the highest order,
and German Wikipedia says the order he cited did not exist.
The men followed him.
A local extra sheet quoted by the Berliner Zeitung in 2026 counted
twenty soldiers in the group that reached Köpenick station,
so the sources do not agree on the number.
What they agree on is that the men followed
a captain who had no authority at all.
They boarded a suburban train. Once in Köpenick,
he gave each soldier a mark and had them
lunch at the station. German Wikipedia reports that,
and a second local account agrees on the lunch and the mark.
Köpenick station is still there, and it is still a working stop.
The S3 runs through it on the line between Erkner and Spandau,
and the station fronts Bahnhofstraße and Elcknerplatz.
It opened on 23 October 1842, and its facilities were rebuilt
between 1899 and 1902 for the increasing traffic.
Since March 2023 it has been in a long rebuild,
expected to run into 2027, so check the access before you go.
From the station the group went on by train and on foot
to the town hall, and sealed it off.
German Wikipedia names two officials the captain had arrested: Georg Langerhans,
the mayor, and Rosenkranz, a senior city clerk.
A legal history article also says he sent
the local police chief home to bathe.
That detail makes the afternoon sound like a farce, and it is
one of the few small details the sources give at all.
The sources give few clock times for the afternoon,
so the day has to be told in stages, by place.
The first stage is the building itself,
and the arrests that made the captain's control of it complete.
Then came the money.
The plaque on the wall of the town hall,
to the right of the entrance, names the target.
In translation it reads: on the afternoon of 16 October 1906, the
shoemaker Wilhelm Voigt seized the town treasury as the Hauptmann von Köpenick.
The cash was handed over against a receipt,
and German Wikipedia says the receipt was signed with an invented name,
von Malzahn. The Deutsche Biographie gives that same name
as the one he used when he set out.
The sums differ between sources, so this episode leaves the figure out.
The officials did what the uniform asked, one step after another.
How long could a captain who did not
exist keep a town hall in order?
Quick break. I'm Yusuf, and this is Walk of Berlin.
If you enjoy stories like this one,
come and walk one with me.
My walk, Berlin Then and Now,
goes from the World Clock on Alexanderplatz to Hackescher Markt,
with an archive photo at every stop.
You'll find it at walk of berlin dot com.
The captain did not keep the officials in the building.
He had the mayor and the treasurer taken away,
by rented cab and under guard, to the Neue Wache in Berlin,
after they gave their parole that they would not try to escape.
The Neue Wache, at Unter den Linden 4,
was built by Karl Friedrich Schinkel between 1816 and 1818 as a
guardhouse for the royal palace across the street.
Since 1993 it has been the central memorial of the Federal Republic
of Germany for the victims of war and tyranny.
A guardhouse that once received two officials from a small town
now commemorates the victims of war and tyranny,
and it is a sobering place to stand when you think
about how a costume was once treated as a real order.
The captain then went back to Berlin by train.
German Wikipedia says he had a light beer
at a station restaurant on the way, bought civilian clothes,
and left his sabre at a station in Rixdorf.
It also says he got rid of most of the uniform on
the Tempelhofer Feld, the old airfield in Berlin.
Flights from the airport ended in 2008.
The costume had been assembled in about eight days, from the
first purchases on 8 October to the afternoon of the 16th.
Since 8 May 2010 the field has been a public park,
with a six-kilometre route for cycling, skating and jogging,
grill areas, and a dog meadow.
For ten days the captain was free.
He had the money from the treasury,
a white moustache and a set of civilian clothes.
The authorities did have a warrant.
German Wikipedia and the Deutsche Biographie both give
a reward of 3,000 marks for his capture,
and the Deutsche Biographie says the warrant was
issued on the very day of the takeover.
Picture his position: a free man with a reward on his head,
a town treasury behind him, and still no papers.
The next part of the story turns on a former cellmate,
who had a reason to talk: the reward.
Ten days after the town hall, German Wikipedia says,
police arrested him at breakfast. The same article names the tip-off:
his former cellmate Kallenberg informed the police,
in the expectation of the high reward of 3,000 marks.
The Deutsche Biographie also records that a former cellmate denounced him.
The man who had been the captain was caught not by a
clever trap, but by the oldest kind of tip, the one from
someone who knew him well enough to betray him for money.
Nothing about the arrest needed a uniform at all.
The case went to the Landgericht II in Berlin, the regional court.
On 1 December 1906 the court found him
guilty of wearing a uniform without authority,
of unlawful deprivation of liberty, of fraud and of serious forgery.
The sentence was four years in prison, a figure that a legal
history article and the Deutsche Biographie both give.
The soldiers were a separate matter, handled by military justice.
A legal history article says the press expected a result in
their favour. It does not record the outcome,
so this episode says nothing more about the soldiers.
The city did not see the affair the way the court did.
The Deutsche Biographie says the public welcomed it as an attack on
Prussian militarism, and that public sympathy later pushed the authorities toward mercy.
Think about what the story exposed.
A squad of soldiers had followed a captain who did not exist.
A mayor had gone under guard after giving his word.
A treasury had handed over its cash against
a receipt signed with a made-up name.
Every one of those people had done what a uniform asked,
and the joke was on the uniform,
and on the rules that made people bow to it.
After almost two years in Tegel prison, the Kaiser pardoned him.
German Wikipedia says he was released early, on 16 August 1908.
The Deutsche Biographie says the pardon came under pressure from public opinion,
and a Berlin tourism site and a Berlin history calendar both say
the Kaiser pardoned him early, after almost two years.
Sources differ on the exact day,
so this episode says only August 1908.
The pardon ended the sentence, but it did not end his fame,
and the fame was the one thing he could still sell.
What did the Kaiser himself think of it?
The Berlin tourism site visitBerlin says he was highly amused,
and a Berlin history calendar, at deutschlandmuseum.de,
says he found the affair very amusing. Both are secondary accounts.
This episode did not find a primary document with his own words,
so the reaction is reported, not proven.
What the record does show is the pardon,
which came after almost two years of a four-year sentence.
The Kaiser's amusement and the court's sentence sat
side by side in the same story,
and the story did not end in a cell.
Voigt did not let the story rest.
After his release he performed as the captain in halls,
at fairs and in circus tents, according to German Wikipedia.
The Deutsche Biographie says he sold postcards with his own portrait on
them and recorded his story on a gramophone disc.
The Berlin museum exhibition in the town hall calls
him a real media star of his time.
A wax figure of him was displayed
in a Berlin waxworks from August 1908.
In 1909 he published his autobiography, Wie ich Hauptmann von Köpenick wurde,
which means How I Became the Hauptmann von Köpenick.
He had found the one thing that paid,
and it was the story.
But a legend pays only while people want to hear it,
and the question was how long that would last.
Yusuf again, one more thing before the story goes on.
If you can't join me in person,
my audio walks take you along the Berlin Wall at
Bernauer Straße and through the medieval old town,
at your own pace, on your phone.
They're at walk of berlin dot com.
The story turned into literature through a play.
Carl Zuckmayer's Der Hauptmann von Köpenick,
which he subtitled a German fairy tale in three acts,
opened at the Deutsches Theater in Berlin on 5 March 1931.
Heinz Hilpert directed, and Werner Krauß played the captain.
The play changed the history on purpose.
In Zuckmayer's version the captain's motive is the passport he cannot get,
and in the end he gives himself up.
The real arrest came at breakfast, after a former cellmate's tip.
The plaque on the town hall says that
the play made him a literary figure.
The play carried him onto the screen.
German Wikipedia lists a 1931 film by Richard Oswald,
made the same year as the stage premiere,
with Max Adalbert in the title role,
and a 1997 version by Frank Beyer with Harald Juhnke.
Helmut Käutner's 1956 film with Heinz Rühmann is the one many people
know best, and German Wikipedia lists it alongside the others.
Each new version took the captain out of the
1906 day and put him into a new costume,
and each one made the joke more familiar to people who
had never stood in that town hall at all.
By now the name had become a word.
Germans call a con that wins obedience by
faking an official role a Köpenickiade,
and the plaque on the town hall uses that word too.
So the captain had left Köpenick, the court,
the prison and the stage behind him.
What remained was the man himself, who had been a convict,
then a joke, then a performer,
and every stage of that life turned on the same uniform.
The next part is about where he went,
what he did after the fame, and how his later years ended.
The Berlin museum's own exhibition title sums up the arc:
Vom Sträfling zur Legende, from convict to legend.
He settled in Luxembourg in 1910.
The Deutsche Biographie says he became a Luxembourg citizen and
lived in Luxembourg City from that year on.
German Wikipedia describes a residence permit dated 1 May 1910,
work as a waiter and as a shoemaker,
and a house he bought in 1912.
The Berlin museum exhibition says he died impoverished in Luxembourg.
The Deutsche Biographie gives a different picture of those years,
saying he had reached a certain prosperity there.
The legend had paid him for a while,
at fairs and in print.
His grave, his plaque and the exhibition are
now the places where his story is kept.
He died on 3 January 1922 in Luxembourg City, aged 72.
The plaque on the Köpenick town hall gives the same two dates,
13 February 1849 and 3 January 1922.
He is buried at the Liebfrauenfriedhof in Luxembourg.
German Wikipedia says the grave stone reads HAUPTMANN VON KOEPENICK,
and that it gives the wrong birth year, 1850.
The plaque and the Deutsche Biographie both say 1849.
The same article says a circus bought the grave in 1961, and
that the city of Luxembourg took over its care in the 1970s.
So the grave has a circus and a city in its history,
and it was the city that took responsibility
for it in the end.
So why does Germany still laugh at him?
Because the trick works on the thing a crowd will defer to,
which is a uniform.
A squad of soldiers obeyed a captain who did not exist.
A mayor gave his word and rode off under guard.
A treasury handed over its cash against a receipt.
The laugh has a serious side.
It keeps in view a lesson the story teaches:
a uniform can make ordinary people obey without asking questions.
In 2018 the Tagesspiegel reported that the CDU wanted
the captain placed on UNESCO's cultural heritage list.
The Berlin Senate declined. Its reason, as the paper reported it,
was that the impostor was not suitable as a point of identification.
This year is the 120th anniversary, on 16 October 2026.
The Treptow-Köpenick district's programme runs across three days.
On the 16th, the Hauptmanngarde performs in the Rathaushof at 16:00,
with free entry and donations for the association requested.
At 17:00 an exhibition on the history and
building of the town hall opens.
At 17:45 the 1931 film is screened in the waiting room
of the Bürgeramt, introduced by a film scholar.
At 19:30 the musical plays at the Altstadttheater Köpenick.
On the 17th the Hauptmanngarde performs again at 11:00,
and the musical is the final event of
the programme on the 18th at 18:00.
A Berliner Zeitung piece from September says, in translation,
that the big anniversary party "literally falls into the water",
so check the programme before you go.
If you want to stand where it happened, go to Alt-Köpenick 21,
the address of the town hall in the old town.
The permanent exhibition, titled The Captain of Köpenick:
From Convict to Legend, is run by the Treptow-Köpenick district museum
and sits in the town hall's ticket office,
which the exhibition listing calls the historic site of the events.
It asks why Voigt turned to crime,
and why he was not given a second chance after prison.
The museum lists its hours as daily
from nine until eight in the evening.
Check those hours before you go, because they can change.
Then find the plaque on the wall to the
right of the main entrance. Read it slowly.
It gives the shoemaker's dates, names the treasury he seized,
and says the act went into history as a Köpenickiade.
In front of the building stands the statue by Spartak Babajan,
in place since 1996. The statue,
the plaque and the exhibition all belong to the same building,
which makes the Rathaus a good place to
see most of the story in one visit.
Look at the statue, then at the plaque, then at the doorway.
Stand there for a minute before you go.
That's this week's story.
I'm Yusuf, and if you want to stand where it happened,
my walks and audio walks are at walk of berlin dot com.
phrases.display: my walks and audio walks are at walkofberlin.com.

phrases.text: Next week, another Berlin story.
